```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment  = "#>",
  fig.width  = 7,
  fig.height = 3.5,
  out.width  = "100%",
  dpi = 150
)
set.seed(42)
library(data.table)
library(ggplot2)
library(reCYCLing)
```

The other vignettes run the simulator with its default settings, which means two
of its mechanisms are switched off. This vignette turns them on:

| Mechanism | Parameters | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| **Non-allelic gene conversion** | `p_conversion`, `conv_dist`, `conv_tract`, `p_conv_interchrom` | Overwrites one monomer's sequence with another's. Homogenizes **without changing array length**. |
| **Hotspot feedback** | `hotspot_alpha` | Makes local duplication rich-get-richer: big identical families duplicate more often. **Redistributes** duplications without adding any. |

Both are off by default (`p_conversion = 0`, `hotspot_alpha = 0`), and with
those defaults the engine reproduces the released behaviour exactly.

---

## Gene conversion

In a gene conversion event a **recipient** monomer's sequence is overwritten by
a **donor** monomer's sequence. Nothing is inserted and nothing is removed, so
unlike duplication and deletion, conversion changes *what* is in the array
without changing *how much* is in it. Its effect is homogenization: copies of
the donor sequence replace diverged neighbours, so the array loses diversity but
keeps its size.

Three parameters control it at the array level (`sim_array()`) and at the genome
level (`sim_genome()`):

- **`p_conversion`** — per-monomer per-generation probability that a monomer is
  a conversion recipient.
- **`conv_dist`** — the distribution of **donor–recipient separation**, in
  monomers. Default `gamma(shape = 1, scale = 20)`, i.e. donors are typically
  a few tens of monomers away.
- **`conv_tract`** — the distribution of **tract length**, i.e. how many
  consecutive monomers are overwritten by a single event. Default
  `gamma(shape = 1, scale = 1)`, i.e. usually a single monomer.

### The length contract

The cleanest way to see that conversion does not change array size is to switch
off every mechanism that *can* change it. With `p_local_dup = 0` and
`p_distal_dup = 0` the size governor has no duplication mass to balance, so it
deletes nothing and each chromosome sits exactly on its target.

```{r conv_length}
TARGETS <- rep(300L, 3L)

static_genome <- function(p_conversion, seed = 11, ...) {
  set.seed(seed)
  sim_genome(K = 3L, target_sizes = TARGETS, n_generations = 400L,
             mu_total = 1e-4, init_l = 178L,
             p_local_dup = 0, p_distal_dup = 0, p_exchange = 0,
             p_conversion = p_conversion, ...)
}

plain <- static_genome(0)
conv  <- static_genome(5e-3)

data.table(
  run          = c("no conversion", "conversion"),
  monomers     = c(nrow(plain), nrow(conv)),
  distinct_seq = c(uniqueN(plain$bponly), uniqueN(conv$bponly))
)
```

Identical monomer counts, but far fewer distinct sequences once conversion is
on: the array has been homogenized in place. Turning the rate up homogenizes
further.

```{r conv_rate}
rates <- c(0, 5e-4, 2e-3, 5e-3)
data.table(
  p_conversion = rates,
  distinct_seq = vapply(rates, function(p) uniqueN(static_genome(p)$bponly), 0L)
)
```

### Tract length

`conv_tract` sets how many consecutive monomers one event overwrites. Longer
tracks convert more sequence per event, so at a fixed `p_conversion` a longer
tract homogenizes faster — and still without any length change.

```{r conv_tract}
tracts <- c(1, 3, 10)
data.table(
  tract        = tracts,
  monomers     = vapply(tracts, function(v)
    nrow(static_genome(2e-3, conv_tract = list(type = "fixed", value = v))), 0L),
  distinct_seq = vapply(tracts, function(v)
    uniqueN(static_genome(2e-3, conv_tract = list(type = "fixed", value = v))$bponly), 0L)
)
```

### Conversion between chromosomes

At the genome level, `p_conv_interchrom` is the **fraction of conversion events
whose donor is drawn from a different chromosome** rather than from `conv_dist`
on the same one. The remaining `1 - p_conv_interchrom` follow the
within-chromosome path.

This gives a second, quite different route to cross-chromosome identical
monomers. Inter-chromosomal *exchange* (`p_exchange`) physically copies a
contiguous block from one chromosome into another. Inter-chromosomal
*conversion* copies only sequence, one short tract at a time, into positions
that are already occupied — so identical monomers appear on both chromosomes
with no block having moved and no length change.

```{r interchrom}
n_cross_chrom <- function(g) nrow(g[, .(nc = uniqueN(chrom)), by = bponly][nc > 1])

within <- static_genome(5e-3, p_conv_interchrom = 0)
across <- static_genome(5e-3, p_conv_interchrom = 1)

data.table(
  p_conv_interchrom = c(0, 1),
  monomers          = c(nrow(within), nrow(across)),
  exchange_events   = c(attr(within, "n_exchange"), attr(across, "n_exchange")),
  shared_seqs       = c(n_cross_chrom(within), n_cross_chrom(across))
)
```

With `p_exchange = 0` there is no exchange event anywhere in the run, yet
`p_conv_interchrom = 1` still produces sequences carried by more than one
chromosome.

The two routes leave different signatures. What differs is not *whether* shared
monomers appear but how they are arranged along the chromosome: exchange leaves
them in contiguous runs (the block that moved), conversion leaves them
essentially isolated. Measuring the mean length of a run of consecutive
cross-chromosome-shared monomers shows the difference:

```{r scatter_vs_block}
shared_run_length <- function(g) {
  shared <- g[, .(nc = uniqueN(chrom)), by = bponly][nc > 1, bponly]
  runs <- g[, {
    r <- rle(bponly %in% shared)
    .(len = r$lengths[r$values])
  }, by = chrom]$len
  data.table(n_shared = sum(g$bponly %in% shared), mean_run = mean(runs))
}

routes <- rbindlist(lapply(1:3, function(s) {
  set.seed(s)
  by_conv <- sim_genome(K = 3L, target_sizes = rep(400L, 3L), n_generations = 400L,
                        mu_total = 1e-4, init_l = 178L, p_exchange = 0,
                        p_conversion = 5e-3, p_conv_interchrom = 1)
  set.seed(s)
  by_xch  <- sim_genome(K = 3L, target_sizes = rep(400L, 3L), n_generations = 400L,
                        mu_total = 1e-4, init_l = 178L,
                        p_exchange = 0.2, exchange_chunk_mean = 200)
  rbind(cbind(route = "conversion", shared_run_length(by_conv)),
        cbind(route = "exchange",   shared_run_length(by_xch)))
}))

routes[, .(n_shared = mean(n_shared), mean_run = round(mean(mean_run), 2)), by = route]
```

Runs of shared monomers are roughly twice as long under exchange. The contrast
is blunted by mutation — an exchanged block stops being identical monomer by
monomer as it ages — so it is the recently exchanged blocks that carry the
contiguous signal.

A practical caveat: homogenization by unbiased conversion runs on a coalescent
timescale proportional to (array size)/rate, so the inter-chromosomal path
*seeds* cross-chromosome sharing rather than building deep identical families
across chromosomes.

---

## Hotspot feedback

By default every monomer triggers a local duplication with the same probability
`p_local_dup`, so duplications land uniformly along the array. `hotspot_alpha`
makes that probability depend on how successful a monomer's sequence already is:

$$p_i \;\propto\; (\text{same-chromosome identical-family size of monomer } i)^{\alpha}$$

and the whole vector is then **rescaled so that the expected number of
duplication events per chromosome is unchanged**. This is the important part:
`hotspot_alpha` is *mean-preserving*. It does not add duplication mass — it only
decides where that mass lands, concentrating it on families that are already
large. That is a rich-get-richer feedback which builds hotspots, and because the
mean is preserved it is not confounded with `p_local_dup` and does not disturb
the size governor's balance.

Family membership is tracked by **lineage**: every copy (local, distal,
exchanged, converted) joins its source's family, and a monomer **leaves its
family as soon as it accumulates a substitution**. So families are transient —
they grow by duplication and are eroded by mutation.

`hotspot_alpha = 0` disables the mechanism entirely and reproduces the released
behaviour exactly.

```{r hotspot_sims}
hot_sim <- function(alpha, seed) {
  set.seed(seed)
  sim_genome(K = 2L, target_sizes = rep(400L, 2L), n_generations = 400L,
             mu_total = 1e-4, init_l = 178L,
             p_local_dup = 5e-3,
             local_dist = list(type = "fixed", value = 1),
             del_dist   = list(type = "fixed", value = 1),
             hotspot_alpha = alpha)
}

runs <- CJ(alpha = c(0, 3), seed = 1:3)[, .(g = list(hot_sim(alpha, seed))),
                                        by = .(alpha, seed)]

fams <- runs[, .(family_size = g[[1]][, .N, by = .(chrom, bponly)]$N),
             by = .(alpha, seed)]
sizes <- runs[, .(total = nrow(g[[1]])), by = .(alpha, seed)]

merge(sizes[, .(monomers = mean(total)), by = alpha],
      fams[, .(largest_family = max(family_size),
               families_ge_5  = sum(family_size >= 5)), by = alpha], by = "alpha")
```

Two things happen at once. The largest identical family gets substantially
bigger with the feedback on — but the standing monomer count barely moves,
because the governor's deletion rate is derived from `p_local_dup` and the
feedback did not change how many duplications happened, only which monomers they
happened to.

```{r hotspot_plot}
ggplot(fams[family_size > 1],
       aes(x = family_size, fill = factor(alpha))) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 1, boundary = 0.5, position = "identity",
                 alpha = 0.55) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(2, 14, 2)) +
  scale_y_continuous(trans = "log1p", breaks = c(0, 1, 3, 10, 30, 100, 300)) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("0" = "grey40", "3" = "firebrick"),
                    name = "hotspot_alpha") +
  labs(x = "identical family size (monomers)", y = "number of families",
       title = "Hotspot feedback lengthens the tail of the family-size distribution") +
  theme_classic()
```

The feedback does not change the number of duplication events; it changes their
distribution, pushing the family-size distribution's tail out to the right.

---

## Using both together

The two mechanisms are independent and compose freely, and — as everywhere else
in the package — a fixed seed reproduces a run exactly.

```{r combined}
both <- function() {
  set.seed(99)
  sim_genome(K = 3L, target_sizes = TARGETS, n_generations = 400L,
             mu_total = 1e-4, init_l = 178L,
             p_conversion = 3e-3, p_conv_interchrom = 0.5,
             hotspot_alpha = 2)
}
identical(both(), both())
```

---

## Parameter reference

| Parameter | Function | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `p_conversion` | `sim_array()`, `sim_genome()` | `0` | Per-monomer per-generation conversion probability |
| `conv_dist` | `sim_array()`, `sim_genome()` | `gamma(1, 20)` | Donor–recipient separation, in monomers |
| `conv_tract` | `sim_array()`, `sim_genome()` | `gamma(1, 1)` | Tract length, in monomers |
| `p_conv_interchrom` | `sim_genome()` | `0` | Fraction of conversions whose donor is on another chromosome |
| `hotspot_alpha` | `sim_genome()` | `0` | Exponent of the mean-preserving local-duplication feedback |

Note that gene conversion is implemented in the C++ backend only; in
`sim_array()` it therefore requires `backend = "auto"` (the default for
substitution-only runs) or `backend = "cpp"`.
